Wall Street collapses: the Nasdaq loses 5.5% in one session, wiping out a little over $2 trillion of stock market value

On Thursday, November 5, the Nasdaq plunged 5.5% to 24,315 points, its worst session since April 2025, and entered a "correction". The S&P 500 lost about 4.3% and the Dow Jones 3.4%. Investors fear a slowdown in AI investment after the Democrats' victory in the midterm elections [1][2][3].

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 24,315.00 points (−5.5%), more than 10% below its last record: that is the definition of a "correction". The S&P 500 fell about 4.3% to 7,358.13 points, and the Dow Jones by 1,833 points (−3.4%) to 51,521.28, erasing all of the previous day's gain [1][2].

The "Magnificent Seven" (Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Tesla) lost more than $1 trillion in market value in a single session, according to CNBC. Nvidia shed almost 9% (more than $440 billion), which turns it negative for the year; Tesla fell 10.8%, Meta 3.9%, Microsoft 3.6%, Alphabet and Amazon 2.2%, Apple 1.5% [2].

Overall figures vary by outlet: CNN speaks of $2.5 trillion of market capitalization wiped out, Benzinga of $2.2 trillion, with the VIX fear index up 39% [3][5]. On the New York Stock Exchange, 2,344 stocks fell against 416 that rose, nearly six to one [2].

The explanation put forward by CNBC and NBC: fear that the construction of data centers for artificial intelligence will slow after the midterm results, which the Democrats won in Congress, with newly elected lawmakers and governors who could tighten the rules [1][4].

Bad company news added to the pressure: Qualcomm lost more than 9% after a disappointing forecast tied to the memory shortage, and Intel, despite a 78% jump in data center sales last week, had already been punished on the stock market for a weaker-than-expected forecast linked to the same shortage [1].
The day before, on Wednesday, November 4, the Dow Jones had nevertheless gained 3%: Thursday's session therefore erased the post-election relief within twenty-four hours [2].

Key point: it is not a bad economic statistic that is sinking the stock market, it is a doubt about the future of artificial intelligence. A large part of Wall Street's recent rise rests on the idea that the tech giants will keep investing massively in data centers. If that spending slows, the expected profits of Nvidia and its suppliers have to be revised down, and so do their shares [1][2].

What makes the fall violent is that many investors had the same bets: when everyone sells at the same time, prices drop all at once. The session also hit almost the whole market (nearly six stocks falling for every one rising in New York), not just tech [2][3].

The link with politics is an analysts' hypothesis, not a demonstrated fact: no law has been passed, and the Democrats have not yet proposed anything specific. Markets are reacting to a fear, not to a decision [1][4].
Another point of caution: the losses in billions of dollars are stock market value, not money actually lost by companies. That value can come back as fast as it left, or not [3].

If you have a PEA, a unit-linked life insurance policy or a world index fund, part of your savings is exposed to the American tech giants: you have probably seen a drop on your statement. One session changes nothing for a ten-year investment, and we neither say to buy nor to sell.

Asia plunges in Wall Street's wake: Seoul loses more than 8% intraday, Tokyo enters a "bear market"

On Friday, November 6, Asian stock markets fell after Wall Street's tech crash: the Kospi lost more than 8% intraday and triggered a circuit breaker, the Nikkei plunged more than 6% and now sits more than 20% below its June peak, and Taiwan's market lost about 8 to 9% [1][2][3].

In Seoul, the Kospi index lost more than 8% intraday and triggered a circuit breaker that suspended trading, falling below 5,000 points for the first time since February. SK Hynix fell about 11.7% and Samsung Electronics almost 10%, according to BeInCrypto; these are intraday figures, not closing ones [1][7].

The day before, on Thursday, November 5, the Kospi had already ended down 5.3% with the triggering of a mechanism suspending program trading. Foreign investors sold 20.6 trillion won of Samsung and SK Hynix shares (about 10.9 trillion for SK Hynix and 9.7 for Samsung), according to Korean outlet MoneyToday [4].

In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 fell 6 to 6.7% depending on the outlet and dropped below 57,000 points, more than 20% below its June 2026 peak: the definition of a "bear market" [3][8]. Advantest, Tokyo Electron and Kioxia, suppliers to the chip industry, suffered the biggest falls [3][8].

SoftBank Group, heavily exposed to artificial intelligence, lost about 9 to 14% depending on the readings, after also being weakened by China's blocking of its takeover of ABB's robotics division [5][8].
In Taiwan, the Taiex index opened about 9% lower and chip giant TSMC fell 7 to 10% depending on the moment of the session [2][6].
Analysts link the fall to Wall Street's (Nasdaq −5.5%) and to fear that US political measures could slow data center construction [1][6].

Key point: the economies of South Korea, Taiwan and Japan are tied to the electronic chip. Samsung, SK Hynix, TSMC and their suppliers make the components that equip American data centers; when Wall Street doubts AI, their shares suffer the same shock, often stronger [1][2].
For Korea, the effect is massive: Samsung and SK Hynix weigh heavily on the Seoul stock market, and foreign investors had already sold more than 20 trillion won of their shares on Thursday [4].
Circuit breakers are automatic mechanisms that suspend trading for a few minutes when a fall passes a threshold, to let investors catch their breath. They do not prevent the fall: they slow it [2].
Caution: the exact closing figures for Friday, November 6 are not yet in the articles we consulted; those on this page are intraday levels and may change [1][3].

If you hold stocks or a world equity fund, part of it contains the big Asian tech stocks. If you buy a phone or a computer, the rise in the price of memory chips also feeds through to device prices, independently of stock markets.

Vance blames the Republicans' rout on the Iran war, and oil falls below $95

After the Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance writes that "the reason we lost is the war". Donald Trump calls his remarks "largely true" but defends his choice. Brent lost 8.7% on Wednesday, to $94.62 [1][2][3].

In a post on social media, JD Vance wrote that the Iran war is the reason for the Republicans' defeat, as they lost both chambers of Congress. According to NBC and CBC, he also cites the cost of living, inflation and the US relationship with Israel [1][4].
Asked at the White House on Wednesday, Donald Trump called these remarks "largely true" while defending his decision to attack Iran, according to ABC News [2].

Brent lost 8.7% on Wednesday, November 4, to close at $94.62 a barrel, and US crude WTI at $88.12. Analysts quoted by CNBC think this result gives Donald Trump a bigger incentive to strike a deal with Iran [3].

According to Gulf News, Donald Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that he had no immediate plan for strikes. On Thursday the 5th, Brent touched its lowest level in about two months before rebounding slightly on Friday, with buyers staying alert to tanker attacks [5].

On the Iranian side, the position remains that the Strait of Hormuz stays closed until the United States ends the war and meets its conditions. The Revolutionary Guards claimed that two tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in the strait [5].
Qatar continues its mediation between the two sides, as our previous day's story on Iran's "unconvincing" response recalls [5].

Key point: for the first time, the war openly weighs on American domestic politics. When the number two of the executive publicly explains an election defeat by a conflict, pressure rises to end it or get a deal quickly [1][3].

Markets understood the signal before the diplomats: Brent went from about $104 to $94.62 in one session without any agreement being signed. The barrel is pricing a higher probability that the strait reopens, not a fact [3].
But nothing is settled: Iran maintains its conditions and incidents continue on the water. A single attacked tanker is enough to reverse the trend within hours [5].
What each side says should be read with distance: Vance's statements are a political analysis of his party, not a verdict of voters, and Iran's are negotiating positions [1][5].
If you drive or heat your home with heating oil, a barrel under $95 is good news for your prices in a few weeks, but the drop can reverse quickly. Don't count on it for your November budget.

France: after the strike, Lecornu gathers unions and employers on Monday at Matignon, with no minimum wage increase decided

The day after a national strike over wages, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called a "social conference" with unions and employers for Monday, November 9. The Interior Ministry counts about 575,000 demonstrators, the CGT 1.6 million. No increase in the minimum wage has been decided at this stage [1][2].
On Thursday, November 5, the Interior Ministry counted about 575,000 demonstrators in France, including 65,000 in Paris. The CGT claims "nearly 1.6 million", including 350,000 in Paris [1].

The ministry reports 448 arrests, 53 law enforcement members injured and 86 firefighting interventions at 6 p.m., while judging that the march of the declared processions went "globally well". Tensions were reported in Paris, Lyon, Rennes and Toulouse [1].
The leaders of the CFDT and the CGT hailed "a success". The mobilization was about wages and the cost of living, with a demand for a rise in the minimum wage (Smic) [1][2].

Sébastien Lecornu announced a social conference on Monday, November 9 at Matignon with employee and employer representatives, to "provide answers to questions of purchasing power and wages", according to Matignon [2][3].
He asked Labor Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou to finalize the ongoing consultations by Sunday; David Amiel continues talks with civil service unions [2].

The general secretary of Force Ouvrière, Frédéric Souillot, said that today "living on an income below 2,000 euros, you can't make it" [2]. According to a source cited by Europe 1, no Smic increase has been decided yet [2].

Key point: the government is responding to a heavily mobilized street by opening a negotiation with the social partners. The open question is whether Matignon will put a boost to the Smic on the table: unions demand it, and nothing has been decided at this stage [2][3].

The gap between the ministry's and the CGT's figures (575,000 versus 1.6 million) is classic: each side counts in its own way, and neither is neutral. Let's retain that the mobilization is significant, without choosing between the two [1].
The context is inflation: energy is pulling prices up in the euro zone, at 4.0% in October according to Eurostat, which eats into purchasing power and fuels wage demands [4].
Caution: what will be decided on Monday is not known, and options mentioned in the media may not materialize [2].

If you earn the minimum wage or close to it, Monday's conference could lead to an increase, but nothing has been announced. What doesn't change: your prices at the pump and on your bills depend mostly on oil and gas.

Ukraine: Brussels brings Americans and Europeans together on reconstruction, three-way talks planned in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11

On November 4 and 5, the European Commission brought together Ukraine, the United States, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, NATO and the World Bank in Brussels to discuss reconstruction and security guarantees. Russia, which was not invited, kept up its strikes. United States–Russia–Ukraine talks are planned in Abu Dhabi [1][2][3].

On November 4 the European Commission hosted representatives of Ukraine, the United States, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, NATO and the World Bank, without Russia, to refine post-war economic development scenarios and identify financial instruments for reconstruction and investment [1][2].

Rustem Umerov, Ukraine's chief negotiator, said discussions were continuing for a second day at NATO headquarters in Brussels. The Commission presents the meeting as a follow-up to meetings organized by the United States in Miami in October [1][2].
The same day, the Commission said Ukraine has made significant progress toward European Union membership and that it expects all remaining negotiating chapters to be opened by the end of 2026 [3].
Three-way talks between the United States, Russia and Ukraine are planned for November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi [3].
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine exchanged air strikes, according to the Associated Press [2].

Giorgia Meloni wrote to European Council President António Costa that the multiplication of negotiating formats makes Europe "less credible" in ending the war, according to the summary of Euronews's November 5 front page [4].

Key point: diplomacy has two tracks that cross. On one side, Europeans and Americans are preparing the post-war period (money, investment, security guarantees). On the other, negotiators are trying to sit at the same table as Russia, in Abu Dhabi. These two tracks must fit together for a peace deal to hold [1][3].

For the European economy, reconstruction is a huge stake: who finances it, with which public or private money, and which companies take part. The Brussels discussions aim precisely to find suitable financial instruments [1].

Meloni's letter touches a real problem: between Americans, Europeans and EU institutions, several discussion formats coexist. She argues for a clearer European voice; the position of other capitals is not known at this stage [4].
Caution: no financing figure was announced at the end of these two days in the articles we consulted [1][2].

If you are a French taxpayer, Ukraine's reconstruction will be financed partly by European and national budgets: the subject will come back in budget debates. For energy and prices, a peace deal would be rather good news, but it is not imminent.

Who will replace Christine Lagarde at the ECB? Applications close Friday, finance ministers discuss them Monday

Christine Lagarde will leave the European Central Bank on February 7, 2027, nine months before the end of her term. Euro zone countries are nominating candidates: applications close on Friday, November 6 and the Eurogroup finance ministers review them on Monday, November 9 [1][2].
According to Euronews, Christine Lagarde announced she would leave on February 7, 2027, cutting her eight-year term short by almost nine months [1].
The euro zone is choosing its candidates: applications close on Friday, November 6, and euro zone finance ministers are to review them on Monday, November 9. It is not yet a vote [1].

The final choice falls to European Union leaders, once the European Parliament and the ECB Governing Council have given their opinion. It needs the support of at least 16 of the 21 euro zone countries, representing at least 65% of its population [1].
Klaas Knot, former president of the Dutch central bank until 2025, is cited among the main contenders. Bundesbank president Joachim Nagel also comes up in several accounts [1][2].

A report published in February said Christine Lagarde was considering this early departure to let Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz choose her successor together; according to that report, a candidate must be able to count on the support of both Germany and France [2].
Meanwhile, the ECB faces euro zone inflation of 4.0% in October, and markets are considering a rate hike at its December 17 meeting [3].

Key point: the future head of the ECB will decide interest rates for twenty countries, which affects loans, savings and the value of the euro. The choice is therefore as political as economic, and a Franco-German agreement is needed for it to pass [1][2].

The departure date matters: Christine Lagarde leaves as inflation is rising and a rate hike is being considered for December. Her successor will inherit an ECB that may be about to raise its rates [3].

The candidates' profile will matter: a former Dutch governor like Klaas Knot or the Bundesbank president do not carry the same political weight in Paris and Berlin, and both capitals must agree [1][2].
Caution: the official list of candidates has not been published in the articles we consulted, and names cited in the press may not run [1].

If you have a variable-rate mortgage or a loan project, the line of the ECB's next leadership will affect your rates in the years to come. In the short term, it is the December decision that matters, not this choice.

Chips have their worst session since 2020: AMD loses 17%, Nvidia nearly 9%, 28 stocks out of 30 in a bear market

On Thursday, November 5, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.3%, its worst session since March 16, 2020. AMD lost 17.4%, Intel 10.4%, Nvidia nearly 9%, and Qualcomm more than 9% after a disappointing forecast tied to the memory shortage [1][2][3].

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunged 12.3%, its worst session since March 16, 2020; according to Benzinga, 28 of the index's 30 stocks are now in a bear market, meaning more than 20% below their peak [1].

AMD gave up 17.4%, Intel 10.4% and Nvidia 8.9%, according to Investing.com; CNBC speaks of more than 9% for Nvidia, which loses more than $440 billion in market capitalization and turns negative for the year [2][3].

Qualcomm had published its results the day before: its earnings per share forecast for the current quarter is $2.15 to $2.35 on revenue of $10.4 to $11.2 billion, versus $2.27 and $10.48 billion expected by analysts. Sales in its phone division fall 26% year on year to $5.1 billion, and its gross margin drops to 52.4% [4].

Intel, which had announced last week a 78% jump in its data center sales, was punished on the stock market for a weaker-than-expected forecast linked to the memory shortage, according to CNBC [2]. AMD said this week that its data center sales had more than doubled [2].
The trigger is the same as for Wall Street as a whole: fear that data center construction will slow after the midterm elections, with possibly stricter regulation [3].
The next day, the fall spread to Asia: SK Hynix and Samsung lost about 10 to 12% intraday in Seoul, TSMC 7 to 10% in Taipei [5].

Key point: a chip stock is worth the profits the market expects in the future. Even rising results (AMD, Intel) are not enough if forecasts disappoint or if future demand becomes uncertain: the price falls because the future is revised down, not the past [2][4].

The memory shortage is the common thread: it makes components costlier for phone and computer makers (Qualcomm, Apple) and limits the sales of those who can't find enough chips. It is a supply problem, not a demand problem, according to Qualcomm's management [4].

The scale of the shock, the chips' worst session since March 2020, shows how much these stocks had become the heart of the American stock market. When they fall, they drag almost the whole index with them [1][3].

If you have a world fund or a Nasdaq ETF, chips weigh heavily in it: the value of your portfolio has probably fallen this week. We do not explain here what to do with your savings, only why things are moving.

How it works: why rising results can make a stock plunge

A stock's price is not a snapshot of the last quarter: it is an estimate of all the profits the company will make in the years ahead. When management publishes forecasts ("guidance") below what analysts expect, the market recalculates: if future profit falls a little, the company's value falls a lot, especially when the stock was expensive. On top of that comes the herd effect: many investors hold the same stocks; when some sell, prices fall, which forces others to sell to limit their losses. That explains a 12% drop of a whole sector in one session. A "correction" means a fall of more than 10% from the last record, a "bear market" a fall of more than 20% [1][2][3][4].

China blocks SoftBank's $5.4 billion takeover of ABB's robotics unit, and SoftBank loses 9% on the stock market

According to the Financial Times, Chinese authorities have prohibited SoftBank's takeover of Swiss ABB's robotics division, a $5.375 billion deal signed in October 2025. ABB confirms the ban for its business in China, but says the two groups are still talking; SoftBank's share lost 9.3% [1][2][3].

SoftBank had agreed in October 2025 to buy 100% of ABB Robotics for about $5.375 billion. The unit made about $2.3 billion in revenue in 2024, about 7% of the ABB group, and employs about 7,000 people [2][3].
The Financial Times reported that Chinese regulators told SoftBank they would not allow the purchase [1][2].
ABB then confirmed it had been informed by SoftBank that the Chinese office in charge of foreign investment security review "has prohibited the acquisition of the ABB Robotics business in China" [3].

The deal had passed China's competition review in February 2026; it is the security review that blocks it, with concerns over the transfer of assets developed in China to a Japanese company and possible leaks of robot-related data [3].
Sources differ on the state of the deal: ABB says the two companies are continuing talks to move it forward, and SoftBank is reportedly considering refiling its application [3].
SoftBank's share lost 9.3% to 3,611 yen on Friday, a move also tied to the tech fall and to Arm Holdings (about −5% the day before on Wall Street), of which SoftBank owns about 90% [3][4].

Key point: a big acquisition must be approved in each country where the target company is present, and a single "no" can stop everything. Here, the Chinese refusal concerns ABB Robotics' business in China, and ABB confirmed the ban [1][3].

The reason given is not competition but security: Beijing does not want technologies developed in China to pass under foreign control. It is an instrument that has become common in the technology rivalry between major powers [3].
For SoftBank, it is a blow to its robotics strategy tied to artificial intelligence, announced by its founder Masayoshi Son. The share was already weakened by the fall in AI stocks [2][4].

If you work in industry, ABB's robotics equips factories in Europe and Asia: the stake is who will control these technologies. For your savings, this is just one of the week's shocks on AI-linked stocks.

How it works: why a country can block a takeover between two foreign companies

When one group buys another, each country where the latter has significant activity can examine the transaction from two angles. The "competition" angle checks that the purchase does not create a monopoly. The "national security" angle checks that the purchase does not give a foreigner control of technologies, data or infrastructure considered sensitive. A single refusal is enough to block the part of the deal located in that country, and often to sink the whole thing. Contracts therefore provide for a deadline and sometimes a termination fee. For markets, these blocks are a risk: the buyer's share price rises before the deal and falls when it moves away [1][2][3].
Takeovers blocked by China: precedents
August 2023

Intel gives up buying Israel's Tower Semiconductor for $5.4 billion for lack of approval from the Chinese regulator, after extending the deadline twice; Intel pays Tower a $353 million termination fee [5].
A $5.4 billion deal can fail at the last deadline because of a single regulator; the buyer may pay a fee [5].
Chinese regulators blocked Qualcomm's $44 billion purchase of NXP Semiconductors, according to Global Finance [6].
Precedents between big American companies and China show Beijing uses its approval right as leverage in technology rivalries [6].
